title: Avowal and Repentance
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley's main teaching emphasizes the importance of acknowledging and taking responsibility for our individual actions as part of a larger web of interconnected suffering. They encourage us to let go of guilt or shame by confessing and repenting, rather than dwelling on past mistakes, in order to work towards healing and awakening both individually and collectively. By recognizing our interconnectedness and releasing attachments to outcomes, we can experience freedom and connection to the world around us, ultimately leading to liberation from karmic conditioning.

sentences.text: Good morning everyone.
Nice to see so many people in our combined sanghas and [unclear: "sordid"] friends.
Today I'd like to talk about atonement and karmic conditioning.
In other words, how did we get here in our state of the world today, and how might we go forward?
We recite a verse every morning in sesshin three times.
We recite it at our precept gatherings.
We recite it every Sunday at our place.
It's often called the verse of formless atonement, but it's all about our karmic conditioning, acknowledging that.
It goes like this.
The first three lines are about our karmic conditioning and the last line is aval.
Ancient twisted karma.
It's a favorite phrase for many people.
There are other translations, but we always come back to that poetic expression of entanglement and perhaps regret.
All of our karma is entangled and twisted and not set.
From beginningless greed, hate, and delusion, the three poisons, the three difficulties, the three sources of our suffering.
Born through body, speech, and mind, those are the three ways that we create karma, that we acquire karmic conditioning: actions of the body, speech, and thought.
I now [unclear: "flee aval"].
And again, aval is a word that is translated in various ways.
Sometimes it says repent, but aval in our current way of speaking about things, it's a nice word.
It opens us.
It acknowledges it all.
It says, "I know, here it is."
Part of that karmic conditioning, part of that entanglement that we notice in our world today, that we all share in, is the karmic conditioning of racism, misogyny, genocide, exploitation.
We live in the midst of this karmic conditioning, and we are not apart from it.
We carry the conditioning through the culture that we grew up in, the past history of our country, the beliefs and the reactivity and the mental patterns that we acquire as we're growing up.
Sometimes we might like to think that other people have those difficulties and not us, but as soon as we do that, we get into trouble.
My wife has a couple of grandchildren that we see frequently these days, and I was thinking about how wonderful and alive and fresh they are.
Then I was contemplating that in families all over our country, and of course all over the world, there are young children growing up that are equally alive and fresh and wonderful.
And then I wondered, well, at what point did they grow up to be a Trump supporter?
It seems like when they're young, they can't be a Trump supporter.
And they're really beautiful and alive at each stage, but at some point do they cross a line, enter the monolithic group of Trump supporters that we have created?
Of course not.
So in addition to carrying this entanglement of bias, we also create groups, we create us and them, and we forget that each individual, just like the children, is fresh and alive.
There's really no point, no line that we can point to when they cross over to be part of this monolithic other.
We talk about repentance, we even talk about confession and repentance, and we'll see those words again a little bit later.
Confession means here acknowledgement: this is how I am, this is how we are.
And repentance means what?
It means knowing I can do better and hoping to do so in the future, trying to do so in the future, perhaps vowing.
Unless this feels like a weight of misdeeds that we carry around, that's not really the case in our Buddhist thinking.
Katagiri Roshi says we are already embraced by the 10,000 things, by the one.
So we have to live our life in the realization that we are already forgiven.
This is not about saying "I'm bad, please forgive me."
It's about saying "I'm connected, and I acknowledge that.
Let's all take a look and see what needs to be done."
Shohaku Okumura, in his chapter on this verse, subtitles the chapter Awakening to Incompleteness.
That's pretty nice: awakening to our individual incompleteness and awakening also to our interconnected wholeness.
Confession and repentance, I've come to really appreciate that over years of practice.
During the period of zazen just prior to the talk, I needed to relocate from the dokusan room to the library so Tim could do dokusan back there.
As I was moving my stuff, I dropped my kutsu, made a big noise, clatter, clatter.
Those of you who were in the zendo certainly noticed that.
My first reaction was horrified.
But rather quickly, okay, I can return to the present.
I can let that be in the past, but still, a little bit agitated.
Then when I got into the other room and thought about it for a moment, I thought, oh, I can put it in my talk.
I can confess it.
It can be a shared event.
Maybe people will even laugh.
And that makes it much better, doesn't it?
It actually makes it something that connects me rather than something that isolates me.
So it has a real power.
Part of our practice is to create the forms in which this so-called confession and repentance can occur in a way that is uniting and healing.
Okumura also says:
*Vow and repentance are inseparable.
When we closely look at our past deeds, we cannot help but repent.

When we awaken to the total interpenetrating reality of our being and look to the future, we cannot refrain from making the vow to live with all beings and to practice according to Buddhist teaching.*
We really see them closely.
When we really acknowledge them...
So today I'm looking at this atonement, this confession and repentance that we can do together, as a solid platform from which we can address the things that need addressing in the world.
Unless we have this solid platform of atoning for our own ancient twisted karma, we're a little wobbly and off balance.
So it feels good to me, a platform from which to act.
I mentioned that our verse is often referred to as the verse of formless atonement.

But Okumura, in his book Living by Vow, a beautiful book on investigating the deeper implications of our often repeated verses, and I don't have it with me, says really this verse is about formal atonement.
That is atonement in the form world, atonement for our deeds in what we call everyday life.
Of course, there's a lot there, so it's worth doing over and over again.
But he says there's another verse for what he calls formless atonement.
So it's curious that we have used the word formless atonement to apply to the verse we recite.
Of course, these are just words, but Okumura's explication helps us see things a little more carefully.
This formless atonement, I think, focuses on a deeper, more imprinted and intractable kind of karma, the karma of perhaps being a human being.
He cites a verse for this formless atonement.
Apparently it comes from the Samantabhadra Sutra.
It goes like this:
*The ocean of karmic hindrances arises solely from delusive thoughts.
If you wish to make repentance, sit in upright posture and be mindful of the true reality.
All misdemeanors, like frost and dew, are melted away in the sun of wisdom.*
*If you wish to make repentance, sit in upright posture and be mindful of the true reality.* All misdemeanors, and that's a catch-all for our deep karma.
He doesn't mention felonies, but I think we can extrapolate.
They're all, like frost and dew, melted away in the sun of wisdom.
Of course, we could just zone out in zazen and think that we've taken care of everything, but we're all beyond that, right?
We are investigating closely and deeply our karmic conditioning.
One of these, I think, deeper aspects of conditioning, this deeper habit, this deeper tendency, is this us-and-them phenomenon.
Me and you, the creating of another being or set of beings that we are in opposition to, like Trump supporters, or you name it, right?
It's very common and easy to see, but so deeply ingrained that even though we see it a hundred times, we fall back into it.
This morning, I think it was during the second period of zazen, the room had quieted down.
Then I heard this noise.
It was like a rhythmic movement on this coarse fabric of zabata.
I thought, I wonder who's doing that and why are they doing it?
I fully appreciate when someone has to rearrange and kind of says, we're all in this together and we're all working as hard as we can.
But this noise, somebody would really have to be trying almost to do this.
I imagined a foot moving back and forth, or a toe.
Somehow I was thinking toe.
Then maybe it was a breath of cooler air from the window.
I figured out, oh, it's water dripping.
It's water splashing.
And then I could relax, right?
Because there wasn't this being over on the other side.
It was on this side of the zendo, by the way, because I was over here.
There wasn't this other being that was the source of my distress that I had created.
Totally imaginary being going.
The water, somehow that was just fine.
So I think we do this.
I know I do.
I have several examples, but since I had a fresh one this morning, I'll use that one.
It's just like this us and them.
We create this imaginary them and believe in it fully, believe that it's the cause of our distress.
It's our own creation, just like that being on the other side of the zendo was my own creation.
While the beings in our world that we find ourselves in opposition to may not seem imaginary, there is certainly an imaginary aspect to them.
We imagine our opponents to be monolithic.
They imagine their opponents to be monolithic.
And we end up clashing with imaginary beings, one set of imaginary beings clashing with another.
I don't know how that works, actually.
Not to say things don't need to be addressed, things don't need to be done.
Not to say suffering doesn't exist.
Not to say we don't have our work as Bodhisattvas cut out for us.
It seems to me another example of this deeply grooved karma, almost part of being human, perhaps inseparable from being human, is our attachment to outcome.

In Tim's talk yesterday, he was reading a talk by David Loy, who said one of the most important things, perhaps, that Buddhism or just people can offer to the world is action without attachment to outcome.
That's what I was trying to suggest in the words I spoke in the zendo last night.
What we aspire to in a Bodhisattva is that they just keep helping.
It doesn't matter which direction the situation is going.
It doesn't matter how things are evolving.
To the Bodhisattva acting in this moment, excuse me, it's just beings needing help, helping.
And that is, I would suggest, liberating.
Because we don't have to tally up our success.
We don't have to talk about our doomsday scenarios, although they might light a little bit of fire under us.
But we just help.
Do what we can.

As I was suggesting last night, in zazen, in this sitting upright, in upright posture and being mindful of the true reality, this is where we can closely investigate our us and them and our attachment to outcome.
To me, as I was sitting the last day or so, that effort without attachment to outcome, effort without figuring, as Dogen puts it, what is that?
The closer I get to experiencing that, the more I think that it is beyond the self.
We can taste it there by letting go of our attachment to outcome, our attachment to success, our attachment to greed, anger and ignorance, or say, grasping and aversion.
When we really look close and let that effort flow, I would suggest that our small self, our attached separate self, is maybe not even there.
And what's happening there?
Then there is activity without attachment, without karmic conditioning, without this entanglement of karmic conditioning that is ourselves.
So it seems to me in the last day that this is a doorway.
Not only is it perhaps what the world needs most, but it is a doorway to our own liberation, our own unburdening of all these entanglements.
And I think we can really only investigate it in zazen, zazen and more zazen, like we are doing here this weekend.
Until those slightest turnings, those slightest attachments float up for our acknowledgement.
And when we see them, they can let go.
Maybe just for an instant, just a taste of that freedom, a taste of that open-hearted giving, so that the bodhisattva energy arises, bodhicitta arises.
And it is not burdened by our karmic conditioning, by our attachment to outcome, by our deep-seated tendency to create an [unclear: "asana"] of them.
But it's right there in any action that we do when we look closely.
I'd like to touch on another kind of repentance.
This is one of Dogen's famous writings, Eihei Kosohotsugamon, which is about Dogen's vow, about Dogen's arousing the vow.
In the closing paragraph, he says:
*Melts away the root of transgressions.
This is the pure and simple color of true practice, of the true mind of faith and the true body of faith.*
Quietly explore the farthest reaches of our karmic conditioning.
And boy, they do go far, don't they?
The more we see, the further they go.
But those entanglements can present themselves to us, in sesshin in particular, for us to allow, for us to unburden ourselves from.
Here again, we have the image of melting away, revealing and disclosing, repenting.
The power of this revelation melts away the root of transgressions.
And there's that language there, we don't like it so much these days, but it melts away our karmic conditioning.
It melts away our obstacles to fully engage.
Maybe the most interesting part of it to me these days is the line that says:
*Repenting in this way one never fails to receive profound help from all Buddhas and ancestors.*
That's kind of a Dogen-esque line, right?
Receiving profound help from all Buddhas and ancestors.

In our class at Seattle Soto Zen this fall, we were looking at how Buddhist practice engages with modern life and where there might be a rub and where there might be an investigation to clarify the practice that we want to do, that we want to offer.
One of the things we looked at was, well, what is this thing about secular Buddhism?
What does that mean?
And what would be lost, if anything, if we move toward this thing called secular Buddhism?
A lot of people find it attractive.
But I think one of the things that would be lost is this profound help from all Buddhas and ancestors.
Because that's kind of out there.
But you can say profound help from the cosmos, from the universe, from all beings, from whatever expression you want to come up with.
But profound help from a larger, deeper, more powerful other.
So that maybe gives us pause.
Do we really believe that?
But for me this is what makes this spiritual or religious, whatever word.
It's important to me and I think it's important to us, to humanity.
I like to call it being lived by the one life.
And again, this repentance, when the karmic conditioning drops or subsides and this effort without desire, without figuring emerges, that's not really something we're doing, right?
Because we're kind of disappearing with that karmic conditioning.
But somehow this effort without desire emerges.
For me, that's the profound help from all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and ancestors.
That's the profound help from Buddha, from the cosmos, from the one life flowing.
And that is encountered by looking so carefully at our karmic conditioning.
Got a little story here from The Hidden Lamp, a collection of koans about and by women with commentaries by women.
It goes like this:
*An old woman asked Master Zhaozhou, "I have a body that contains the five obstacles.
How can I be free of the world of suffering?"
Zhaozhou said, "Pray that all beings are born in heaven and that you yourself suffer forever in a sea of hardships."*
That's pretty, yeah, she was probably sorry she asked the question.
I'd like to ask somebody else, if you don't mind.
But what is being pointed to here?
Like all of us, she asked, how can I be free of the world of suffering?
But Zhaozhou, being the lightning-lipped teacher that he is, says, pray that all beings are born in heaven.
That is, pray that all beings are helped and taken care of.
And that you yourself suffer forever in a sea of hardships.
That's pretty extreme.
This is kind of an exaggeration, perhaps, for the sake of effect.
But Diane Rosetta, who wrote the commentary in the book on this koan, says about Zhaozhou:
*He says, allow yourself to suffer in the very ways you see as obstacles.
And by entering deeply that very suffering, through the suffering of a body, you will find a way to help others.*
In this commentary, Diane Rosetta takes up the particular suffering of a woman's body.
Since I don't know about that, I will just refer it to your investigation.
The chapter is called Zhaozhou and the Old Woman's Obstacles.
But we all have bodies and it all creates suffering.
So enter deeply that very suffering.
As we've been talking about, enter deeply this karmic conditioning.
See it, clearly receive it.
Be forgiven for it.
Allow it to enter your body and allow it to settle.
This karmic conditioning is the site, as in S-I-T-E, the location, the point at which we can be liberated.

Without our karmic conditioning to atone with, we have no way to go beyond it, to experience this liberation, to allow this effort without figuring to flow, or to even power us for a short moment, or to deeply enter that very suffering, that suffering that you see as obstacles.
So deeply entering it is atoning with it, repenting it, bringing it forward for us all to investigate together.
For us all to discover that we share it, to look at it carefully, to see that it melts away before our acknowledgement, our deep [unclear: "zha zhen"] mind acknowledgement.
If I could sum it up, I would suggest that our atonement is a platform for us going forward, and our karmic conditioning is the site of our liberation.
It is not separate, it is required.
That's what [unclear: "Zha Zhe"] says about, please hope that you are born in a world of suffering, because that is the fuel, the possibility for entering this one life, for being unburdened.
And while being unburdened, the bodhisattva energy, effort without figuring, emerges.
So we have to do it together, and we're doing it.
So please continue doing it.
